questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the molecular property that makes water wet a polar surface
questions.stem: A design team needs a protective coating that spreads a thin film of water across a solar mirror instead of letting it bead up. Which property of water produces that behaviour?

options.text: Water is polar, so its partial charges hydrogen-bond to the glass and pull the film outward.
Water molecules are tiny, so gravity drags thin films flat across any polished surface.
options.misconception: believes gravity and molecule size control wetting

options.text: Water is dense, so heavy droplets are forced to spread instead of forming rounded beads.
options.misconception: believes density, not polarity, prevents beading

options.text: Water dissolves silica slowly, which erases the raised edges that would trap droplets.
options.misconception: thinks water dissolves glass to flatten droplets

questions.explanation: Water's partial charges hydrogen-bond to the charged glass, so it wets and spreads instead of beading. Gravity, density and glass solubility do not govern wetting, so those readings misidentify the operative property.
questions.hint: Think about what draws water onto a charged surface.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a surface tension trend in terms of hydrogen bonding
questions.stem: In a bench test the force needed to break a water surface of fixed width fell steadily as the sample warmed from 10 °C to 60 °C. What does that trend indicate?

options.text: Water loses its polarity as it warms, so molecules stop bonding to each other.
options.misconception: believes warming destroys molecular polarity

options.text: Thermal motion weakens the hydrogen bonding that holds surface molecules together.
Hotter molecules travel faster, so the surface film thins and tears more easily.
options.misconception: blames faster molecular motion for the loss

options.text: Warm water is less dense, so there is simply less material resisting the pull.
options.misconception: explains the trend by density change alone

questions.explanation: Surface tension comes from attraction between surface molecules, so a weaker breaking force means that attraction is weakening. Heating never removes polarity, and neither speed nor density explains the trend.
questions.hint: Ask what holds surface molecules to their neighbours.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a single polar molecule solvates both ions
questions.stem: In a coolant additive study, sodium ions are said to be surrounded by water molecules that point their oxygen ends toward the ion. Explain why a single water molecule can help solvate both a positive and a negative ion.

answer.exemplar: Water is polar, so each molecule carries a partial negative oxygen end and a partial positive hydrogen end. The oxygen end is attracted to a positive ion while the hydrogen end is attracted to a negative ion, so the same molecule can orient differently in each case and both ions end up surrounded by ordered shells of water.

questions.explanation: One water molecule has opposite partial charges at its two ends, so it can point its oxygen at a cation and its hydrogens at an anion. That is how one molecule solvates both kinds of ion.
questions.hint: Orient the two ends of one molecule in two different ways.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why pure water conducts poorly despite being polar
questions.stem: A team is told that dissolving salt makes water conduct electricity, and asks why pure water does not. Explain the role of molecular polarity in the conductivity of pure water.

answer.exemplar: Water is polar, so its molecules contain separated partial charges that could in principle carry current. In pure water almost no ions exist, so there are almost no charge carriers and the conductivity is very low. Dissolving salt supplies mobile sodium and chloride ions, and it is those ions, not the polar water molecules, that carry the current.

questions.explanation: Polarity gives water separated charges, but pure water contains almost no mobile ions, so it carries little current. Salt contributes mobile ions, and those ions rather than the polar solvent do the conducting.
questions.hint: Separate solvent polarity from the actual charge carriers.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain a heating comparison using specific heat capacity
questions.stem: A cookware engineer claims a cast iron pan heats faster than a water-filled pan of the same mass. Explain what specific heat capacity contributes to that comparison.

answer.exemplar: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram by one degree. Water has a much higher value than cast iron, so the same mass of water needs far more energy for each degree of rise. That is why the water-filled pan warms slowly and stays cool at the stove, while the drier cast iron pan responds quickly to the flame.

questions.explanation: Water's high specific heat means more energy per degree rise, so a water-filled pan changes temperature slowly. Heat capacity, not conductivity or mass alone, explains why the cast iron pan responds faster.
questions.hint: Compare the energy each material needs per degree.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why capillary rise is greater in narrow tubes
questions.stem: A design brief asks why water rises higher in a narrow glass tube than in a wide one, and requests an explanation that connects tube width with the height reached.

answer.exemplar: The rise is produced by the balance between the pull of adhesion to the tube wall and the weight of the column that cohesion keeps together. In a narrow tube the wall holds a proportionally larger amount of water per unit length, so a greater weight can be lifted for the same surface pull. Widening the tube spreads the same wall force over a longer, heavier column, so the height reached falls.

questions.explanation: Adhesion to the wall supports the column while cohesion keeps it connected, and a narrow tube presents more wall per unit height. That is why the column rises further in narrow tubes and less in wide ones.
questions.hint: Compare wall contact area with the weight of water lifted.

questions.topic: Water: Solubility of Salts and Oils
questions.learningObjective: Explain contrasting solubility of salt and soap in water
questions.stem: A packaging engineer needs a rinse that removes grease from a machine part yet still rinses clean with plain water. Explain why soap and salt behave so differently in water.

answer.exemplar: Salt dissolves in water because the water molecules are polar and can form ion-dipole attractions with the separated sodium and chloride ions, which then disperse throughout the solution. Soap molecules have a long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail that water cannot surround or solvate well, so they gather into micelles with the grease in the middle and the polar heads outside, and the whole assembly washes away with rinsing water.

questions.explanation: Salt is ionic and is dispersed by polar water molecules binding its ions, whereas soap carries a nonpolar tail that grabs grease and is carried off in micelles. Charging the tail would not make it dissolve grease.
questions.hint: Compare what each substance has that water can solvate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain freezing point depression through ion hydration
questions.stem: A formulation chemist asks why adding table salt to water makes the water freeze at a lower temperature than pure water, and wants the molecular reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Dissolving salt separates sodium and chloride ions into the water, where each ion is surrounded by an ordered shell of polar water molecules. Because these hydrated ions occupy space and disrupt the orderly hydrogen-bonded structure of liquid water, the molecules can no longer pack into a crystal as easily, so a lower temperature is needed before ice forms. This is the standard explanation of freezing point depression by a dissolved solute.

questions.explanation: Hydrated ions disrupt the hydrogen-bonded lattice that pure water forms on freezing, so more cooling is needed and the freezing point falls. The effect comes from solute particles, not from changed polarity.
questions.hint: Ask how the solute interferes with crystal formation.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain slow acidification of exposed water using polarity
questions.stem: A lab manager asks why pure water stored in an open beaker slowly becomes slightly acidic over weeks, and wants the role of polarity explained.

answer.exemplar: Pure water is polar, so its molecules can act as both hydrogen bond donors and acceptors. Carbon dioxide in the air dissolves into the water and reacts with it, producing carbonic acid and additional hydrogen ions, which lowers the pH. The polarity of water is what allows this reaction to occur, because it lets water molecules donate a proton and stabilise the charged products. The change is slow and small, but it is real.

questions.explanation: Water is polar, so it can donate protons and stabilise charged products, letting dissolved carbon dioxide form carbonic acid and free hydrogen ions. Polarity permits the reaction.
questions.hint: Ask how water can act as a proton donor.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the work needed to create a new water surface
questions.stem: At 20 degrees Celsius the surface tension of water is 0.0728 newtons per metre. How much work in joules is needed to create 10.0 square metres of new water surface at that temperature?
questions.explanation: Work against surface tension equals surface tension times new area, so 0.0728 newtons per metre times ten square metres gives 0.728 joules. Dividing rather than multiplying gives a far too small value.
questions.hint: Multiply surface tension by the area created.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain harbour temperature moderation using specific heat
questions.stem: A harbour engineer notes that the water in the bay stays milder overnight than the surrounding built-up shoreline, and asks why the difference occurs.

answer.exemplar: Specific heat capacity is the energy required to change the temperature of a given mass by one degree. Water needs far more energy per degree than land materials such as concrete and asphalt, and a large mass of water also releases a lot of stored energy as it cools. That combination means the harbour warms and cools more slowly than the built-up shore, so nights there stay milder. The effect is about heat capacity, not about the harbour being shaded from the sun.

questions.explanation: Water's high specific heat and large mass mean it changes temperature slowly and releases stored heat slowly, keeping the harbour milder overnight. Land materials heat and cool quickly because they need far less energy per degree.
questions.hint: Compare energy needed per degree for water and land.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain soil water movement in terms of pore size
questions.stem: A soil scientist needs to explain why fine sandy soil transports water upward better than coarse gravel, and asks for the capillary explanation in terms of pore size.

answer.exemplar: Water rises through a pore network because adhesion to the pore walls pulls water upward and cohesion keeps the column connected. In fine sand the pores are small, so the same wall pull supports a proportionally larger column and the water climbs higher, matching the smaller capillary rise height that goes inversely with pore radius. Coarse gravel has wide pores where the wall pull is spread over a heavier column, so the water rises less far and drains more freely under gravity.

questions.explanation: Adhesion to pore walls plus cohesion in the column drives the rise, and the rise height grows as pores shrink, so fine soil lifts water further. Coarse pores spread the pull over a heavier column and drain faster.
questions.hint: Think about how much wall area meets the water.

questions.learningObjective: Explain blotting action using the capillary principle
questions.stem: A paper designer needs to explain to a client why blotting paper lifts a stain from a surface but a smooth plastic sheet does not, and wants the capillary principle stated.

answer.exemplar: Blotting paper contains many fine fibres, and the spaces between them act as a network of narrow capillaries. Water is drawn into these spaces because adhesion to the fibre walls pulls it upward while cohesion holds the column together, so the stain travels up the sheet and is held there. A smooth plastic sheet has no narrow pores and no wetting surface, so the liquid simply spreads as a film and is not lifted away.

questions.explanation: Blotting works because many narrow pores give adhesion to wall plus cohesion in the column, drawing liquid up into the fibres. A smooth sheet has neither narrow pores nor a wetting surface, so nothing is lifted.
questions.hint: Compare the pore structure of the two materials.
